sentences.back: The physics of how airplanes fly is a fascinating combination of engineering and natural forces.
At bottom, flight relies on the principle of lift, which is an upward force that counteracts gravity.
This lift is mainly produced by the shape of the airplane's wings, often called airfoils.
When air flows over the wing's curved upper surface, it has to travel a longer distance than the air flowing along the flatter lower surface.
To cover this longer distance in the same amount of time, the air above the wing moves faster.
According to Bernoulli's principle, faster-moving air exerts less pressure than slower-moving air.
As a result, the pressure beneath the wing becomes greater than above it, pushing the wing upward; this is lift.
Another key force is drag, which resists the airplane's motion through the air.
Drag is caused by air friction and the air's resistance as the plane passes through it.
Engineering plays a crucial role in reducing drag by designing streamlined shapes for the fuselage and wings.
The more streamlined an object is, the less drag it experiences.
Think of the difference between pushing a flat board through water and pushing a sharp knife through water; the knife meets less resistance as it cuts through.
Likewise, airplanes are designed to "cut" through the air efficiently.
The plane's engines provide thrust, the forward force that pushes the plane ahead, and thrust in turn makes air flow over the wings and produce lift.
Without enough thrust, there won't be enough airflow to create the pressure difference lift needs.
Once lift exceeds the plane's weight, it can take off and fly.
Pilots constantly adjust engine power and the positions of control surfaces such as ailerons and elevators to control lift, drag, thrust and weight, keeping flight stable and controlled.
Understanding these basic principles of physics is essential for designing safer, more efficient aircraft.
It is an ongoing process of innovation, finding ways to maximize lift and minimize drag for every kind of aircraft, from small private jets to large commercial airliners.
